Issued at 221 AM EDT Mon Aug 24 2026

With clear skies overhead this morning, observation stations are 
already showing temperatures dropping into the 40s and even mid to 
upper 30s across the western half of the U.P., with the Baraga Plains 
RAWS site already down to 37F as of 1 AM EDT. Should this trend 
hold, there could be multiple spots in the western interior U.P. 
that see lows bottom out in the mid to potentially even lower 30s, 
allowing patchy frost to form (particularly elevated sfcs). In 
addition, there could be some patchy fog over the far west as warm 
air advection aloft moves overhead, but confidence on fog occurrence 
is still somewhat low even now given the lack of it being seen 
upstream in northern WI and MN on satellite. After the sun rises 
today, expect fairly calm and quiet weather as high pressure ridging 
moves overhead. While we should be warmer than we were yesterday, 
with antecedent cooler air taking time to move out of the area, 
thinking highs will generally stay within the 70s. Gusty NW winds 
over Lake Superior will keep dangerous waves and rip currents over 
the beaches of Alger County today, so another Beach Hazard Statement 
is in effect throughout the entirety of today over there. The 
swimming conditions along the Marquette County shoreline are better 
today due to the shore's geometry protecting it somewhat from NW'rly 
winds. Nevertheless, some rip currents and hazardous waves are still 
expected along the beaches of Marquette County, so swimmers should 
still exercise caution and not get into the water unless they are 
experienced swimmers as the rip currents and waves could still tire 
out people fast. 

Moving into tonight, expect the generally quiet weather to continue 
as clouds build in from the west with time via an approaching 
Clipper low. Given the continuing WAA, lows tonight are expected to 
not be as cool as they are this morning; that being said, some of 
the coldest spots in the interior central and east could drop down 
into the mid to upper 30s thanks to mostly clear skies for the 
overnight hours. In addition, with WAA continuing in the lower to 
mid-levels of the atmosphere, some fog is possible over mainly the 
interior central and east tonight as temperatures cool to around the 
dewpoint. Should the fog form, we could see visibilities of 1/2 mile 
or less, which could create traveling/visibility concerns for the 
morning commute for those going to work and/or school. 

Our next shot of rainfall looks to arrive over the western U.P. on 
Tuesday as the Clipper approaches. While global/medium range 
guidance is more reserved on the start time of the rainfall, some of 
the CAMs do show showers starting as early as the mid-to-late 
morning hours over the far west given the modest isentropic lift 
moving into the area. That being said, with not much diurnal 
instability to work with, I have my doubts as to rain chances 
starting that early. Therefore, have the precipitation chances 
capped at around 30% between 8 AM and 2 PM EDT over the west half on 
Tuesday. As better diurnal instability develops over the area and a 
LLJ develops and brings some support by the afternoon hours, shower 
and thunderstorm chances increase over the west half. While the best 
shearing and helicity are projected to be south of us in northern 
WI, thinking it may not be totally out of the realm of possibility 
for a stronger (but sub-severe) thunderstorm or two to occur. As the 
showers and storms continue and spread into the rest of the U.P. 
Tuesday night and Wednesday, expect the rainfall chances to become 
maximized to ~80 to 90% as the low's center moves through Lake 
Superior. The additional forcing from the low with PWATS 1.25 to 
1.50 inches could bring heavy rainfall at times, although QPF 
guidance is fairly muted for the most part on rain totals with this 
event. Therefore, while it does seem like most, if not all, of the 
U.P. will see at least some rainfall, given the convective nature of 
the precipitation not everyone will see similar amounts; as of now, 
the NBM currently has a 50 to 99% of a quarter inch of rainfall 
occurring between Tuesday morning and Thursday morning, with the 
greatest chances over the east and interior west whereas the lowest 
chances are in the south central. The rainfall chances look to 
generally end over the area by late Wednesday as the Clipper lifts 
northeast towards James Bay. However, some CAA behind the low could 
kick-off some light lake effect rain showers over the area on 
Thursday, but accumulations would be very small as high pressure 
builds in from the west once more. 

High pressure ridging returns to the U.P. once again by Friday, 
allowing for dry weather to return to the area. Moving into this 
upcoming weekend there really isn't a good signal for the 
precipitation chances as some upper level ridging continues to build 
into the area, even as troughing starts to move back in at the sfc 
late this upcoming week
